title: Docker vs virtual machines
idea: A virtual machine (VM) runs a whole operating system on virtual hardware. A container is an isolated process that shares the host's kernel.

analogy.text: VMs are houses, containers are apartments. Each house has its own foundation. Apartments share one, the kernel, but each has a locked door.
analogy.breaks: Apartment walls are solid; a shared kernel is a thinner boundary.

points: A hypervisor is software that shares one machine's hardware among VMs.
Each VM boots its own operating system and kernel; containers use the host's kernel.
So a container starts as a process, with just the files your app needs.
On Mac, Docker Desktop runs a Linux VM to host your containers.

pitfalls: Do not rely on containers alone to contain untrusted code; they share the host kernel.
Need a different kernel, such as Windows on a Linux host? Use a VM.

quiz.q: A Linux server runs three containers. How many kernels are running?
options: Four: the host's and one per container
One, shared by the host and all containers
None; containers run without a kernel
quiz.why: Containers are isolated processes. They all use the host's kernel; only a VM boots a kernel of its own.

takeaway: Containers share the host kernel; VMs bring their own.
